title: The Impact Square: Four Levers of Human Responsibility from Conversational to Agentic AI
affiliations: Carinthia University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: The Impact Square: Four Levers of Human Responsibility from Conversational to Agentic AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Access to generative AI has become close to universal, yet the outcomes people obtain from it diverge sharply. Existing explanations locate the divergence either in the system-capability, interface, communication style-or in broad constructs such as AI literacy. Neither specifies what a user actually does, within a single interaction, that makes the difference. This paper develops the Impact Square, a theoretical contribution that decomposes a human-AI interaction into four levers under human control: task, model, context, and prompt. The decomposition itself is not the claim. It rests on an attribution of responsibility: the user is answerable for each of the four levers and for the adequacy of the result they accept, and this answerability is not reduced by the competence of the system. Formed under conversational use, the framework is tested against the paradigm shift under way. We show that the levers do not migrate to the system as work becomes agentic; they change instantiation along four dimensions-the frequency at which they are set, the scope over which they act, their visibility, and the cost of correcting them-and extend the analysis to agent populations, accumulated context, model routing and initiating systems. This yields the central claim: the four levers are invariant under changes in interaction paradigm, because they are the points at which intention enters a process that cannot generate intention. We state what would refute that claim, map the levers onto validated AI literacy instruments, and derive seven testable propositions.

title: Vigilance Unbundling: How Cognitive Automation Reallocates Error-Containment Capacity

detail.title: Vigilance Unbundling: How Cognitive Automation Reallocates Error-Containment Capacity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Research on complex accidents, high-reliability organizations, resilience engineering, safety citizenship, distributed cognition, and expert judgment already shows that safety is not produced by formal controls alone. It is also produced by situated people who notice weak signals, remain uneasy after nominal checks pass, pursue unresolved concerns, challenge instructions, and sometimes continue investigating beyond the apparent economic value of a problem. The same human variability also causes error, unsafe improvisation, alarm dismissal, and normalization of deviance. The argument is therefore not that human idiosyncrasy is intrinsically safe. It is that operational roles can jointly produce task output and a mixed portfolio of discretionary behavior, some of which arrests rare failure trajectories. This paper identifies a transition created by cognitive automation. Before automation, a situated human role may impose a positive lower bound on adaptive inquiry as a co-product of participation. Automation can preserve or improve the formal task output while relaxing that nonseparability constraint. Safety cognition must then be purchased as a separate control input. A minimal model yields two conditional results. First, if the pre-automation inquiry floor exceeds the organization's unconstrained preferred level, automation strictly reduces adaptive inquiry even when prices, preferences, and hazards are unchanged. Second, where audit-legible controls and open-ended inquiry compete for shared organizational capacity, increasing the private return to auditability raises legible control while reducing open-ended inquiry; total safety activity can nevertheless rise. This paper calls these transitions vigilance unbundling and legibility substitution. The paper then derives an architectural and governance implication. AI-heavy systems may need synthetic idiosyncrasy: deliberately engineered heterogeneity in anomaly sensitivity, inquiry persistence, and stopping rules. Such a detector is ineffective without commitment-protected standing: evidence access, resources, reporting paths, and authority to slow or interrupt production. The framework predicts a possible divergence between improving compliance scores and declining performance on seeded weak-signal tests. It also proposes empirical designs that separate stopping-rule diversity from ordinary ensemble diversity and protective human discretion from generic morale effects. The paper is a theoretical synthesis and research program, not evidence that synthetic idiosyncrasy has already been shown to reduce catastrophic risk.

detail.abstract: An algorithmic nudge personalizes the choice architecture. Instead of one uniform intervention for everyone, each user gets their own. However, when an algorithmic nudge is superior to a uniform digital nudge remains unclear. In a field experiment with a fintech firm (𝑁 = 4,322), customers were nudged to make an extra contribution to their retirement plan; the recommended amount was either computed by a machine-learning model or uniform. Although the algorithmic recommendations were more accurate than the uniform amount, their average effect on the contribution decision was indistinguishable from zero. Using causal machine learning, we document significant effect heterogeneity: the algorithmic nudge appears to help some customers and backfires for others. The effects on conversion for the two groups differ by 6.0 percentage points (𝑝 = .015). Delivering the algorithmic nudge only to customers predicted to respond positively is projected to raise contributions by 34%. The backfiring concentrates among younger customers new to the savings decision. A more accurate recommendation is thus not automatically the better nudge. Organizations deploying algorithmic nudges need to know whom the nudge helps and whom it should not reach.

title: Agile AI Agentic Neural Based Framework For Complex Workflow Forming, With Multiple Implementations Upon Upstream And Downstream Scenarios

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract:
The oil&gas sector increasingly depends on agile, reliable, and explainable workflow automation to support production and operations activities such as wellbore fault diagnostic, maintenance, and pipeline scheduling. However, existing genAI-based agents technologies are limited by complex workflow forming, lack of cross-scenario generalization, and insufficient continuous refinery mechanisms, which restrict their ability to support long procedure workflows or adapt to evolving operating conditions. This study proposes an Agile Agentic Neural (AAN) framework that autonomously forms, executes, and refines complex workflows. The approach is designed to address upstream wellbore workovers and downstream pipeline scheduling, enabling event sensing, task planning, tools coordination, and continuous improvement through dual human-machine feedforward mechanism. The objective is to establish an operationally robust and scalable approach that accelerates production decision-making while maintaining interpretability and safety across integrated asset operations.
The AAN framework adopts a neural network inspired architecture with 3 layers. The input layer performs scene recognition, semantic understanding, and task decomposition from multimodal field data (e.g., SCADA, production logs), using distributed self supervised distributed agents to ensure quality-grounded fusion. The computational layer organizes sub-agents within dynamically selected topologies—mesh, tree, code or workflow structures based on operational context. A supervisor agent uses in-context refinement and historical success logs to optimize decisions such as diagnostics, workflow planning, and response actions examining. The output layer assembles executable workflows and employs a dual feedforward loop that integrates engineer feedback and machine-observed metrics, enabling digital-twin-like self-refinement without retraining. Validation includes 60 shale wellbore maintenance cases (pump leaks, rod failures, scaling, wax deposition) and pipeline scheduling scenarios within previous couples of years, involving equipment faults, weather anomalies, and supply-demand disturbances. Ablation studies compare four feedback mechanisms to assess robustness.
Across wellbore maintenance tasks, the AAN framework achieved human and agent evaluation scores of 0.76-0.98, with standard deviations <0.1 in event sensing, task planning, agent coordination, and tool use. Pipeline scheduling cases showed
comparable performance, with 0.74- 0.93 accuracy and strong stability under multiphase flow and hydrat risk conditions. Cross-scenario generalization maintained 0.85-0.94 accuracy, though tool usage precision declined in highly heterogeneous cases. Ablation testing confirmed the superiority of the global dual-feedback design, achieving 0.78-0.98 accuracy with the lowest variance (0.02-0.19), highlighting its value for real-time production control and risk mitigation.

title: LLM for Offline Retail Recommendation

detail.title: LLM for Offline Retail Recommendation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Recommender systems are central to online platforms but remain difficult to deploy in offline retail, where the closed-loop behavioral data infrastructure underlying conventional recommenders is largely absent. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) create an opportunity to build recommendation around the natural interaction logic of offline retail, in which customers express their needs directly through language. Realizing this opportunity, however, requires translating open-ended customer requests into accurate product rankings and enabling the recommender to improve across deployment stages. We address these challenges with OffRecLLM, a two-phase LLM-based recommendation framework. The first phase constructs customer requests associated with purchases from retailers' existing data and learns a deployable foundation recommender that first identifies broadly relevant products, then narrows this pool to a smaller consideration set, and finally performs fine-grained residual reranking. The second phase continues learning from authentic customer requests and preference feedback observed after deployment, converting these signals into pairwise preferences and applying direct preference optimization from customer feedback (DPO-CF) while remaining anchored to the foundation recommender. We evaluate OffRecLLM with a large toy retail chain in Asia. The foundation recommender substantially outperforms both structured and LLM-based recommendation benchmarks and 60 experienced sales associates in a source-blind randomized customer experiment. Using customers' authentic feedback from this experiment, DPO-CF produces a preference-optimized recommender that further improves performance in a second randomized customer experiment. Together, these results establish OffRecLLM as a general framework for developing LLM-based recommenders in offline retail, from initial deployment with existing retailer data to continuous improvement through subsequent customer interactions.

detail.abstract: Products, models, and policies are routinely optimized for a representative or average member of the population they serve. We define the Average-Fit Loss (AFL), a population-level functional that quantifies the utility forgone when a single design tuned to the center of a heterogeneous population is applied to that population in full, and we use it to bring several established results from separate literatures under one lens. Under a smooth fit model the AFL equals a dispersion functional of the population, recovering the mismatch cost of address models of product differentiation; in the quadratic case it is the total variance. Once participation is endogenous, the AFL decomposes into an intensive margin (degraded service to those retained) and an extensive margin (exclusion of those pushed below threshold), the latter being the deadweight loss of unserved demand. Because the excluded do not appear in a system's own usage data, any AFL estimate formed from observed users is downward biased, an instance of selection and survivorship bias applied to the measurement of fit: a system cannot, from its own data, see most of its own average-fit loss, and the bias grows with the mass excluded. In more than a few dimensions almost no one is near-average on every relevant dimension, so the loss is borne broadly rather than by a minority. We illustrate these on the ANSUR II anthropometric survey (6,068 individuals, 93 body measurements), the modern descendant of the 1952 cockpit data. The contribution is not a new theorem but a single named metric, and a measurement, that connect product differentiation, welfare economics, and selection bias to the design of systems built for the average. The AFL is the formal complement of the price of fairness: not the cost of imposing accommodation, but the cost of withholding it.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author(s) declare that there is no relevant or material financial interest or conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.

detail.abstract: Decisions made by long-lived software agents are entities with a lifecycle: they are proposed, approved, and realised, they may be superseded, contested, or invalidated by later decisions, and at any moment the question of whether a past decision still holds is an ontological question about the decision itself, not a retrieval question about its text. This paper contributes an ontological analysis of that lifecycle and its formalization as the Decision Lifecycle Ontology (DLO). The analysis distinguishes a decision as an information object from its primary status, a monotonically advancing phase, and from its derived states such as superseded or conflicted, which are relationally determined and may co-occur with any phase; supersession is analysed as an acyclic temporal relation between decision objects, evidence as an information artifact bound by obligation, and ownership as a singular agentive commitment. Five audit axioms make these commitments machine-checkable as executable shape constraints. The ontology is evaluated in the manner of the discipline, by competency questions, of which 16 of 19 are answerable over the operational graph with complete explanation paths, by axiom validation, where every injected violation is detected and one real violation was caught in routine operation, and by cross-domain instantiation, where the unmodified axiomatization transfers to a disjoint domain and surfaces a previously unnoticed supersession cycle. An application study on restart-time recovery quantifies the practical stake; its ablation attributes the gain to the status and time-validity commitments, generalised as a recovery-audit separation principle.

detail.abstract: Do high stock valuations during the emergence of a general-purpose technology such as AI reflect price bubbles? I propose a new framework that measures the AI premium gap–the wedge between objective expected returns from full-information econometric benchmarks and subjective expected returns from analyst forecasts, for AI firms relative to non-AI firms. A negative gap is consistent with bubbles. From 2009 to 2024, the gap is positive. Applied to the dot-com era of the 1990s, the same framework yields a negative gap, consistent with a dot-com bubble. This contrast suggests the AI era differs fundamentally, highlighting the framework's broader applicability.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Listing Stringency Index (LSI), a novel, survey-based composite measure developed using data from 40 World Federation of Exchanges (WFE) member exchanges. The LSI quantifies and compares IPO listing requirements across nine regulatory dimensions, including financial thresholds, governance, disclosure, and operational compliance. It provides a standardized framework to analyse the relative stringency of listing regimes without prescribing optimal regulatory design.
Our findings reveal substantial cross-jurisdictional variation in how exchanges regulate market entry, with particularly wide differences in voting rights, financial criteria, and corporate governance rules. The LSI also captures changes over time, documenting both tightening and relaxation of rules across dimensions—particularly in response to ESG pressures and SME access priorities.

title: Hidden Regions: Regional Innovation Capacity and the Limits of Visibility
affiliations: , Technische Universität München (TUM), Technische Universität München (TUM), Technische Universität München (TUM) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Hidden Regions: Regional Innovation Capacity and the Limits of Visibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no competing interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Dieter Schwarz Stiftung under the project Hidden Regions: Innovation in the Periphery.

detail.abstract: The concept of Hidden Champions has become a cornerstone of innovation and management scholarship, yet the regional conditions that shape and are being shaped by them remain undertheorized. This paper extends the concept from the firm to the regional level by introducing Hidden Regions as a complementary unit of analysis for understanding innovation from the margins of innovation systems. We introduce the concept of "Hidden Regions" to refer to economically strong, innovation-intensive regional innovation systems that constitute the economic backbone of many countries and provide the institutional and socioeconomic environments in which many globally competitive firms, including Hidden Champions, emerge and thrive. Yet Hidden Regions remain weakly represented in dominant innovation narratives, indicators, and policy arenas, and face a particular set of challenges in a rapidly changing global innovation landscape that forces them to confront their hiddenness. We conceptualize this as a capacity-visibility mismatch: Hidden Regions combine substantial niche innovation capacity with limited visibility and recognition. We develop a framework to explain this mismatch by distinguishing between two defining dimensions-innovation capacity and visibility-and six regional conditions that inform their configuration: specialization, institutional thickness, knowledge and learning regimes, embeddedness, peripheral positioning, and accessibility/proximity. We develop the framework through a range of vignettes that contrast Hidden Regions like Heilbronn-Franconia and Mirandola against metropolitan innovation hubs and left-behind regions. By theorizing Hidden Regions as a key factor for national innovation capacities emanating from the margins, this paper contributes to debates on outsider innovation and place and context sensitive innovation policy.

title: Does Generative AI Help or Hurt Publishers? It is Determined by the Contract
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Marketing and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Marketing Area

detail.title: Does Generative AI Help or Hurt Publishers? It is Determined by the Contract

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: A Generative AI engine (Gen-AI; e.g., ChatGPT) adapts content from publishers for individual users, therefore competing with the publishers themselves. We examine licensing arrangements between Gen-AI and publishers for request-specific use of the publishers' content, and how these a!ect publishers' incentives to produce and share content. We study three contracts that are currently being used in such partnerships across multiple industries: a fixed-payment contract where the publisher is paid a usage-independent amount, and two usage-based contracts where, based on the usage of the publisher's content to generate output, the publisher is paid either a per-use unit fee, or a share of Gen-AI's revenue. We show that Gen-AI's profit-maximizing contract is one of the usage-based contracts, and which one it is depends on the value that Gen-AI can add. Gen-AI's optimal contract can induce the publisher to develop and share high-quality content, and can make the publisher better o! than without Gen-AI. Consumer surplus, however, may reduce due to higher content prices as a result of the upstream Gen-AI-publisher partnership. Therefore, depending on the contracting structure, Gen-AI's rise can help publishers and hurt consumers, which is essentially the opposite of the sentiment reported in popular media.

title: Hybrid Otsu–Canny Segmentation with Adaptive Bounding Box Expansion for Object Localization in Baggage X-ray Security Images

detail.title: Hybrid Otsu–Canny Segmentation with Adaptive Bounding Box Expansion for Object Localization in Baggage X-ray Security Images
detail.abstract: Automatic localization of candidate objects in baggage X-ray images is challenging because transmission imaging produces overlapping structures, weak material boundaries, and limited surface texture. Although learning-based detectors have improved X-ray inspection, their development commonly depends on labelled training data and dedicated computational resources. This study presents a training-independent object-localization framework that combines the complementary intensity and structural information obtained from Otsu thresholding and Canny edge detection. An Otsu foreground mask and a Canny edge map are generated in parallel and fused through a logical AND operation to retain edge evidence supported by the foreground-intensity distribution. The smallest enclosing bounding box is then refined using an adaptive expansion procedure that examines intensity changes in successive boundary bands. The method was evaluated on 120 grayscale images from the Baggage X-ray Threats dataset and compared with cropping-loop, Otsu, Sobel, and Canny baselines. The proposed method achieved the highest mean bounding-box intersection over union of 0.873 ± 0.125, compared with 0.842 ± 0.143 for Canny, 0.811 ± 0.130 for Sobel, 0.797 ± 0.156 for the cropping loop, and 0.766 ± 0.141 for Otsu. It also produced the lowest mean squared error (0.0334 ± 0.032), the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (16.47 ± 3.92 dB), and the highest structural similarity index (0.589 ± 0.137). These descriptive results indicate that combining intensity and edge evidence with adaptive box refinement can improve localization relative to the evaluated classical baselines without requiring a learned model.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the speed of price adjustment and the conditional volatility dynamics in the Bovespa Index futures contract (INDFUT) traded on B3 following the release of US macroeconomic announcements (Non-Farm Payroll and CPI). Using a high-frequency dataset with 44,990 1-minute intraday observations covering the period from August 2025 to August 2026, we implement an intraday event study and a joint ARMA(1,0)-GARCH(1,1)-X modeling approach. The results indicate that positive exogenous shocks-data released above market expectations-negatively impact the asset's price (β Pay =-0.2526 and β CPI =-0.3386, both significant at 1%). This mathematically inverse relationship demonstrates that upside surprises in US economic activity and inflation trigger immediate selling pressure in the Brazilian stock market, reflecting capital flight from emerging markets due to the risk of monetary tightening. Furthermore, the larger magnitude of the CPI coefficient highlights that investors exhibit a stronger aversion to inflationary surprises than to job creation data. Additionally, conditional volatility exhibits high persistence (α+β = 0.9828) with immediate uncertainty jumps proportional to the magnitude of the forecast error. The findings support the semi-strong form of the Efficient Market Hypothesis and attest to the rapid external informational contagion on B3's microstructure.

detail.abstract: As healthcare systems are becoming more and more software dependent, such as in the electronic health records (EHRs), clinical decision support systems, and medical device software, a high degree of reliability is required in software validation and testing. Any lack of functionality within these systems can have direct impacts on clinical workflows, patient safety, regulatory compliance and the quality of healthcare services provided. The complexity, scale, and sensitivity to risk of today's healthcare applications can be challenging to test using traditional software-testing methods. This study explores the effectiveness of incorporating risk-based test automation frameworks when increasing software reliability level in a healthcare environment, in a multi-year practitioner study on practical software testing in real-life environments. Amland (2000) has introduced the concept of risk-based testing that prioritizes testing activities based on the risks, business and technical, involved in the testing. Felderer and Schieferer (2014) have pointed out that structured risk classification models are useful for making better test decisions.

detail.abstract: Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) has moved from a novelty product to mainstream consumer finance in the space of a few years. Before 2020, BNPL was a niche offering at the checkouts of online fashion merchants. BNPL then experienced substantial growth (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 2022; Salem & Udis, 2025), coinciding with increased online shopping since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. BNPL is now a pervasive payment option. In 2026, you can use BNPL to delay and split up payments for anything ranging from a pizza to your rent, and many items in between. As the market has grown, so has the academic literature. There is now sufficient research into BNPL to take stock and review what we have learned. In this article, we summarize insights from the economics, finance, and marketing academic literature. While we have learned a great deal about BNPL in the last few years, we also discuss many remaining open questions and current concerns impacting policy decisions. We start by explaining what BNPL products are and the business models of BNPL lenders. Then, we summarize the economics and psychology behind why some consumers use these products. Next, we describe the customer base that uses BNPL. We show the effects of BNPL on consumers, an area of research with substantial policy interest. Another area of policy interest is whether BNPL loans should be reported in a consumer’s credit report. We explain why BNPL is typically not on credit reports and its implications. Finally, we offer some concluding thoughts.

detail.abstract: Time-series momentum (TSMOM)-going long an asset whose own recent trailing return is positive and short (or flat) otherwise-is one of the more robust cross-asset findings in the momentum literature, documented across dozens of futures markets over multiple decades. Early cryptocurrency evidence (Liu and Tsyvinski, 2021) reported a strong Bitcoin TSMOM effect, but on a sample ending in May 2018, before the market structure a retail trader operates in today existed. This note asks two questions the series applies to every strategy: is the effect statistically real in the market regime that can actually be traded now, andwhere the literature's numbers are positive-could a retail trader on a single exchange reach them? Reviewing the most recent, longest, and methodologically strongest crypto-specific test (Grobys et al., 2025; 30 large-cap coins, 2016-2023), the raw TSMOM effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero over the full sample (0.90%/week), marginally positive before July 2020 (1.74%/week, significant only at 10%), and negative and insignificant after July 2020-the regime closest to today. The raw insignificance is driven by a single one-day 1,400% outlier; trimming it restores 1.51%/week (t = 2.63), underscoring heavy tails (power-law tail exponent below 3). A volatility-scaled overlay improves the full-sample figure (1.86%/week) but does not establish a base effect in the current regime for the overlay to improve. On the broader 2,500-coin value-weighted universe the factor is significantly negative (-3.40%/week) and is not reproducible on a single retail venue. Unlike the preceding notes in this series, this hypothesis is closed at the literature stage rather than with an own Binance replication, on the explicit ground that the strongest available study already reports no statistically significant evidence of the effect in the tradable regime. The contribution is a source-verified synthesis and a recency/regime-feasibility argument: a published edge that appears to have aged. This note does not claim trend-following "does not work"; it claims that this specific published evidence is not established as a currently tradable retail edge.

title: Tax Law Scholarship: We need to talk about Methodology

detail.abstract: Tax scholarship draws on many disciplines, such as economics, law, history, political science, philosophy, accountancy and finance, international business, management, psychology, sociology and anthropology. Thus, taxation is inherently a multidisciplinary (or even interdisciplinary) area of research. Traditionally, research in (international) tax law is first and foremost doctrinal research. It is legal technical knowledge of the legal system based on the systematic study of legal texts, such as legislation, treaties, case law and commentaries. However, doctrinal legal research seems to suffer from an image problem as non-lawyers perceive it often to be based on subjective beliefs and value-judgments. A lack of familiarity with legal methodology and methods plays a major role here. Tax law scholars should therefore be more transparent about their methodology. This would also enable a more fruitful academic dialogue with other disciplines in the context of multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary tax research. detail.abstract: Modern economies create money against assets that already exist-land, receivables, sovereign debt, securitised claims. Knowledge, the one input that is non-rival, that carries increasing returns, and that alone can decouple welfare from biophysical throughput, is excluded from the collateral base and funded residually, downstream of the money it helps create. This paper argues that the exclusion is the central structural defect of contemporary macroeconomic governance, and that it explains a cluster of otherwise disconnected pathologies: the appropriability gap in innovation, the secular decline in research productivity, the deadweight burden of grant tournaments, the reproducibility crisis, the collapse of the economics of journalism, the inversion of educational finance, and the chronic under-provision of culture. Wisdom economics is proposed as the discipline succeeding knowledge economics, distinguished by one move: where knowledge economics counts the stock of ideas, wisdom economics prices their direction. A wisdom aggregate W combines a verified increment, a disclosure coefficient and a directional coefficient; new money is issued as a function of W subject to a hard ceiling set by biosphere regeneration. Knowledge determines allocation; the biosphere determines volume. The framework covers four processes-creation, distribution, acquisition and expression-and artificial intelligence, which is not an application of it but a precondition for it: AI simultaneously destroys the wage channel through which knowledge workers were paid and supplies the attestation capacity a knowledge-anchored currency requires. Because AI is trained predominantly on the commons, a principled attribution rule follows directly, and it is a better fiscal instrument than taxing machines. A system-dynamics simulation over 2027-2050 returns a counter-intuitive roadmap: the highest-impact ordering leads with acquisition, not creation, provided a low-cost attestation floor is established concurrently-a result invariant to the assumed initial overshoot. No feasible ordering closes the gap by 2050.

detail.abstract: This report examines the web accessibility of Satisfactory Academic Progress (SAP) webpages across nine University of California institutions. Findings were interpreted in relation to WCAG 2.1 Level A and Level AA accessibility requirements. Accessibility errors varied across campuses, with very low color contrast emerging as the most common system-wide issue. Other error types were comparatively uncommon. Overall, the findings indicate that UC SAP webpages generally contained relatively few accessibility barriers, but recurring issues related to contrast and form controls remain important for remediation. The report recommends that financial aid practitioners collaborate with campus IT, web development, and accessibility personnel to correct verified errors, review interactive elements, and establish recurring accessibility audits so that SAP information remains accessible to students using assistive technologies.

detail.abstract: Exchange rate volatility is among the most significant financial risks facing internationally active small and medium enterprises, yet survey evidence across countries consistently shows that most exporting SMEs use no formal hedging instruments at all. This paper reviews the corporate hedging literaturedeveloped overwhelmingly on large-firm dataand evaluates its applicability to small firms, before synthesising the empirical evidence on SME currency risk management practices and the barriers to derivative adoption. The review organises documented barriers into four categories: scale-driven cost barriers arising from fixed costs and minimum transaction sizes in derivative markets; knowledge barriers rooted in financial literacy constraints of owner-managed firms; relationship barriers reflecting SMEs' limited access to banks' risk-management product lines; and perception barriers concerning the framing of hedging as speculation. The paper concludes that the under-hedging of small exporters is a structural feature of derivative market design rather than simply a firm-level failure, and outlines a research agenda on the rapidly changing fintech-enabled hedging landscape.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes two analytical categories, "economy" and "dyseconomy," to characterize whether a social system possesses the structural capacity to keep the relevant welfare-and-cost coordinates from deteriorating systematically, without relying on sustained exogenous injection. The criterion is not the scale of GDP, the volume of trade, or fiscal capacity, but three system-level operating mechanisms: an effective pricing standard, a discretionary expenditure flow, and local clearing capacity. The paper argues that the three are necessary conditions for that capacity; it does not claim sufficiency. 

     Of the three, local clearing capacity is formalized here as the clearing rate δ—the turnover speed of the inefficient stock, whose reciprocal reads as a half-life—and is connected to the structure of rules. The paper distinguishes enabling rules, which enlarge the set of feasible transactions, from foreclosing rules, which close the channels of entry and exit, and argues that the rule-side marker of de-economisation is not a rise in the total number of rules but a rise in the share of foreclosing rules within the supreme rule set, and that the two classes ought to carry asymmetric institutional rigidity. The pricing standard and the discretionary expenditure flow follow the objects already defined in Paper III of this series (Wang, 2026c); this paper only states their interface with the three conditions. 

       Philanthropisation of the state is one endogenous path toward de-economisation, not the only point of origin; the five stages set out here are a stylized sequence rather than a temporal law, and the historical cases are illustrative mappings. This is a conceptual framework paper; the three conditions await testing by subsequent data research.

title: The Profit-Bias Identity in Sports Betting: Bookmaker Profit as the Public's Prediction Error

detail.title: The Profit-Bias Identity in Sports Betting: Bookmaker Profit as the Public's Prediction Error

detail.abstract: Sports betting moves money continuously from a large public to a small number of firms. The most influential account of that flow, due to Levitt (2004), holds that books price away from the market-clearing point to exploit predictable public biases. It computes profit from two numbers-the probability that a side wins the proposition and the fraction of handle it attracts-treating the share on a side as independent of the outcome. Here we relax that assumption and derive a profit-bias identity: profit is affine and increasing in the expected share of handle on the losing side, with Levitt's expression as the special case of independence. The identity resolves the book's margin into exactly three channels: its hold, the product of its price shading and the public's lean, and the covariance between bet share and outcome. A lean is thus worthless without shading, and shading is worthless without a lean. Under a public-belief model, the profit driver is the public's Bayes error: the probability of a representative bettor selecting the losing side. We provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a "Goldilocks Zone": prices at which book and bettor both profit. Testing these predictions on 1,139 Major League Baseball games, we find that the apparent dependence between bet share and outcome is a Simpson's paradox: present when games are pooled, but absent once they are separated by which side the book favored. The public leans heavily toward favorites, but we detect no matching shading, and the realized margin is indistinguishable from the hold.

detail.abstract: Current planetary health policy institutionalizes "resilience" as a linear progression in which addressing vulnerability through adaptation yields system stability (V → A → R). However, this reductionist framing conflates distinct ecological and geographical traditions, operationalizing health system resilience as static absorptive capacity (the ability to provide sustained care despite environmental shocks), while ignoring transformative resilience. Drawing on general systems theory, complex social-ecological dynamics, and information theory, this commentary demonstrates that treating health institutions as static systems locked in a permanent conservation phase is ecologically and operationally unviable. By misdefining resilience as passive endurance rather than dynamic reorganization across panarchic adaptive cycles, current governance frameworks create severe moral hazards. Specifically, top-down technical interventions fail to alter underlying structural vulnerabilities, instead shifting the ethical and operational burden of climate disruption directly onto frontline workers through labor exploitation and workforce burnout. To navigate accelerating environmental change, planetary health governance must abandon mechanical paradigms of endless absorption. Public health policies must shift toward frameworks of ecological plasticity and transformative capacity, embracing structural reorganization and evolutionary adaptation as necessary conditions for sustainable socio-ecological survival.

detail.abstract: This study, based on a theoretical model, evaluates the optimality of green finance policies for banks, considering three options: (i) mandatory green priority sector lending-the social planner mandates all banks to allocate a fixed minimum portion of total credits to the green sector, (ii) voluntary green priority sector lending-the social planner advises banks to allocate certain portion of total credits to the green sector voluntarily, but imposes a compensatory green tax on those banks which do not invest in green sector to adjust the green credit loss and invests entire proceeds in the green sector, and (iii) green fundingbanks raise funds specifically for green credits. detail.abstract: To index the inequality of outcomes between two different social groups, researchers often summarize the distribution in each group by a statistic such as a quantile or mean, and then compare the resulting quantiles or means. While comparisons of this nature are easy to implement and understand, they may obscure important dissimilarities between the distributions, and as a general approach to the measurement of inequality this practice is ad-hoc and unprincipled. We construct a framework for measuring "distributional inequality" that directly compares the distributions of the two groups and allows researchers to build their normative judgments about inequality into the resulting measure. Building on the inequality literature for one group, we put forth principles that specify inequality is to be measured by the effects of transfers, and we define our measure as the smallest cumulative effect associated with a sequence of transfers that moves the distributions to a state of "equality". We show that tractable measures satisfying these principles can be derived using optimal transport. Inspired by the generalized entropy index for the one group case, we introduce a flexible class of measures featuring a parameter that controls the sensitivity to inequality in the upper and lower tails of the distributions, using these with data from the American Community Survey from 2005-2024 to describe the evolution of the gender wage gap among a) men and women working full time, and b) Black male and Black women in the labor force.

title: On Justice:  James Buchanan and Amartya Sen

detail.abstract:
The sine qua non of Adam Smith’s Moral Philosophy is justice. Justice is the linchpin of “the liberal plan of equality, liberty and justice”, an ideal condition of society that Smith strived to describe in an effort to encourage its approximation.  Given human frailty perfection is impossible, but closer approximation is possible.

James Buchanan and Amartya Sen are self-professed disciples of Smith.  In the Smithian tradition they each see justice as essential to approximating the ideal society.

For James Buchanan the realization of justice is the establishment of a set of rules for market competition that ensure Pareto Optimality, the opportunity of every individual to get the maximum utility from his resources.  

At the heart of James Buchanan’s analysis stands the sovereign individual … homo economicus.  Homo Economicus is amoral.  The only constraints on his choices are those imposed by the rules.  A necessary condition for achieving Pareto Optimality is rules that are just.  According to Buchanan, the realization of this optimal condition requires a constitution that represents the unanimous consent of the sovereign citizens.

Buchanan’s focus on the rules for economic competition sets that competition into a larger context. One-dimensional analysis, Economics, becomes a two-dimensional analysis, Political Economy.

Establishing a consensus on the rules of the game is necessary but not sufficient to realize the liberal plan.  The rules must be followed to be effective.  If the rules must be enforced by the state, the sovereignty of the individual is lost. To his credit, Buchanan recognizes this and adds a socially constructed and inculcated ethic to follow the rules.  Here the social dimension enters his analysis.  But it is an awkward fit.  His homo economicus is amoral and sovereign. Inculcating this moral constraint into Buchanan’s homo economicus through an unconscious shift “produced by the moral suasion undertaken by others” undermines the assertion that homo economicus is sovereign.

Buchanan’s Political Economy is a significant improvement in the scope of analysis. However, there is another dimension vital to telling the whole story – the social dimension.  For a complete analysis of society, one has to include the social dimension.  Doing analysis in three dimensions is to think like a Moral Philosopher, like Adam Smith.   Amartya Sen does this in his work.

 Sen says we should expand our conception of human nature. Humans are not optimizers on a single dependent variable: utility.  Adam Smith’s individuals are more complicated than that.  Smith models individuals as motivated by self-love, justice and beneficence. Sen returns to Smith’s complex individuals.  In Sen’s analysis individuals are motivated by well-being (self-love), and agency, the concern we have for justice and beneficence.  

When there is consensus that the rules are fair and a commitment by all citizens to play by the rules commutative justice can be achieved.  

Communative justice is necessary but not sufficient for a sustainable liberal. plan.  Distributive justice, the unanimous consensus that the distribution of benefits from the Pareto Optimal outcome are just is also necessary for sustainability.  If there is a perception of distributive injustice, those who feel unjustly treated may ignore the rules undermining commutative justice.

Buchanan is focused on commutative justice.  He sees no way to divine the standards of distributive justice so he is agnostic on this dimension of justice.  Sen thinks that there is a need for distributive justice but he is wary of violating the fundamental value of property rights, so he does not offer a clear path forward on this front.

detail.abstract: India's competition law has experienced substantial changes since the Competition Act was passed in 2002. One of the key components is the merger control framework, designed to oversee mergers and acquisitions that may impact competition in the market. This paper provides a thorough analysis of the effectiveness of merger control under India's competition law regime, with a focus on its ability to achieve its antitrust goals. This study utilizes a qualitative approach, conducting a thorough review of relevant literature such as legal provisions, case law, and scholarly articles, to analyze the merger control mechanisms in India. It assesses the legal framework's capacity to tackle anticompetitive practices and encourage market competition. It assesses the practical application of merger control, taking into account the Competition Commission of India (CCI), the effectiveness of the merger review process, and the influence of merger rulings on market dynamics. The results suggest that despite advancements in India's competition law regime regarding merger control mechanisms, there are still some challenges that require attention. These challenges involve the necessity for increased transparency and predictability in decision-making, ensuring the enforcement of merger remedies, and tackling procedural bottlenecks in the merger review process. The study provides recommendations for enhancing the effectiveness of merger control under India's competition law regime, such as boosting the CCI's institutional capacity, simplifying merger review processes, and encouraging stakeholder involvement. detail.abstract: Growing geopolitical risk and reliance on fossil fuels have halted climate mitigation. Finance plays a crucial role for mitigation influenced by the credibility of climate policies. detail.abstract: On 1 January 2026, the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) officially entered its substantive implementation phase, becoming the world's first systematically implemented carbon border adjustment instrument. The CBAM certificate price was set at €75.36 per tonne of CO₂ equivalent in Q1 2026, adjusted slightly to €75.28 in Q2, with Q3 tracking toward the €79-86 range. Concurrently, on 10 July 2026, Russia formally requested the establishment of a WTO dispute settlement panel (DS639), making CBAM the first carbon border adjustment dispute to reach the panel-request stage, with review scheduled for the 25 September 2026 DSB meeting. The EU further plans to expand CBAM to approximately 180 steel-and aluminum-intensive downstream products by 2028, covering machinery, automotive parts, household appliances, and others, with an estimated 7,000 to 8,000 newly affected Chinese enterprises and approximately €18 billion of Chinese exports annually brought under coverage. Based on the complete nine-dimensional theoretical system of Prim-Lex Theory (Economic Climatology)-the Fivefold Prim-Fire, the Three-Tier GC⁴A Constraints, the Five-Element Dynamic Coupling Equations, the Eight-Dimensional Framework, and the Prim-Nexus Guidance-this paper systematically applies the five operational models-REMC (Fire), CLL (Metal), GCSOS (Water), RCE-B/S (Wood), and G-REMI (Earth)-to cross-border carbon compliance governance. It proposes a "Prim-Lex Green Compliance Label" three-color certification system based on nine-dimensional assessment. Using manufacturing in the Yangtze River Delta and Pearl River Delta as empirical cases, this paper demonstrates that through systematic nine-dimensional compliance optimization, enterprises can reduce CBAM certificate purchases by approximately 25%-40% and lower carbon tariff compliance costs by approximately 18%-35%. This paper provides a quantifiable, certifiable, and auditable governance operating system for global carbon markets, green supply chains, and cross-border carbon compliance, while offering a theoretical response from China's independent knowledge system to the WTO legality debate surrounding CBAM in the context of DS639.

detail.abstract: This paper studies dynamic industry allocation with regimes defined as the holding paths a switching-averse investor would have chosen with hindsight, computed exactly by a dynamic program whose single penalty reads as a drawdown–rebound tolerance. A three-layer hierarchy moves layer by layer from aggressive high-beta return seeking to risk protection: each of the 46 Fama–French industries is rotated against a common high-beta anchor, Chips (semiconductors), defensive overlays retreat into refuge assets when the market turns, and a final layer concentrates capital in the most reliable pairs while scaling exposure down in turbulent markets. We also use a pooled XGBoost classifier for universal pair prediction: training one model on the data of all pairs lets the regularities shared across the cross section dominate pair-specific noise, and the cross section of its forecasts serves as the consensus signal that triggers the defensive moves. Out of sample over three decades that postdate every design choice, each layer contributes a distinct increment: the hierarchy nearly doubles the Sharpe ratio of the equal-weighted industry benchmark while cutting maximum drawdown by more than half, outperforms the S&P 500, and beats the identical pipeline run under classical hidden-Markov labels.

title: Mean Reversion, Heterogeneity, and Quasi-Stationary Firm Size Distributions: A Fokker-Planck and Spectral Analysis

detail.title: Mean Reversion, Heterogeneity, and Quasi-Stationary Firm Size Distributions: A Fokker-Planck and Spectral Analysis
detail.abstract: Firm size distributions are frequently interpreted through the lens of scale-free growth, with heavy-tailed outcomes often attributed to multiplicative stochastic dynamics. Recent evidence based on employment and revenue distributions, however, suggests a different picture. Employment distributions exhibit stable characteristic scales and thin tails, while apparent heavy tails in revenue become substantially weaker once economically distinct firm populations are analysed separately.This paper develops a stochastic framework that reconciles these findings within a unified representation of firm-size dynamics. We formulate a generalized Fokker-Planck equation combining diffusion, drift, turnover, and interaction effects, and identify a mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as a natural benchmark for quasi-stationary firm-size distributions. The benchmark generates Gaussian distributions in logarithmic size characterized by an equilibrium scale and finite variance, consistent with the dominant empirical regularities observed in firm-level data.Using a similarity transformation, the dynamics are mapped onto a Hermitian operator whose spectrum governs relaxation toward the quasi-stationary state. This representation yields explicit propagators, response functions, and autocorrelation structures. The analysis shows that empirical parameter estimates imply weak mean reversion and relaxation times measured in decades rather than years. As a result, observed firm-size distributions should be interpreted as persistent quasi-stationary states continuously perturbed by entry, exit, heterogeneity, mergers, technological change, and other economic shocks.The framework also provides an alternative interpretation of apparent heavy tails. Aggregation across heterogeneous quasi-stationary populations broadens distributions and increases tail mass without requiring fundamentally scale-free growth dynamics. Local scale invariance and global mean reversion therefore emerge as complementary rather than competing descriptions of firm growth.

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Israel Science Foundation (Grant No. 1621/23).

detail.abstract:
A tax return can be more than a calculation of a taxpayer's liability. In a system that requires taxpayers to self-report, it is also a collection of tax positions, each embodying a legal claim regarding how statutes, regulations, and judicial doctrines apply to a particular transaction. Most tax positions are routine. Some exploit legal uncertainty. A smaller and more consequential category openly challenges prevailing interpretations of the Internal Revenue Code (Code), urging the Internal Revenue Service (Service) or the courts to adopt a different interpretation.

Recent developments have fundamentally altered the environment in which taxpayers formulate and report tax positions, making it increasingly important to revisit both the concept of tax positions and the regulatory framework that governs them. The first development is the Supreme Court's 2024 decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which overruled Chevron deference and required courts to exercise independent judgment instead of automatically deferring to federal agencies' interpretations of statutes. As a result, Treasury regulations and other Service interpretations no longer receive the degree of judicial deference they once did, increasing the practical significance of tax positions that challenge existing interpretations of the Code. The second development is the substantial reduction in the Service’s workforce, which has diminished its capacity to identify, evaluate, and respond effectively to novel tax positions.

Together, these developments call for a renewed framework for determining both which positions warrant regulatory attention and how they should be regulated. The Article begins by identifying the category of positions that should be the primary focus of the Service's enforcement efforts. Then, focusing on how tax positions should be regulated, the Article distinguishes between tax positions that exploit legal uncertainty and therefore should be deterred ex ante, and tax positions that serve a legitimate law-shaping function and therefore should be permitted ex ante while remaining subject to ex post administrative or judicial review.

Building on this framework, the Article provides guidance for the Service's enforcement efforts and proposes replacing the current interest regime for tax underpayments with one that sets the interest rate above the taxpayer's weighted average cost of capital (WACC), thereby deterring the opportunistic use of tax positions. In doing so, the Article seeks to align the regulation of tax positions with both the post-Loper Bright legal landscape and the practical realities of a resource-constrained tax administration.

title: Regime-Dependent Connectedness, Dynamic Hedging, and Portfolio Optimization across Green Finance, Energy Markets, and Financial Risk Indicators
affiliations: Chung Yuan Christian University, National Yunlin University of Science and Technology and Chung Yuan Christian University

detail.title: Regime-Dependent Connectedness, Dynamic Hedging, and Portfolio Optimization across Green Finance, Energy Markets, and Financial Risk Indicators
detail.abstract: This study provides an integrated framework linking risk measurement with risk management in green finance and energy markets. A rolling Quantile Vector Autoregression (QVAR) connectedness framework is employed to capture state-dependent spillovers across the 0.05–0.95 quantile spectrum, while Dynamic Conditional Correlation Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (DCC-GARCH) models are used to estimate hedge ratios, optimal portfolio weights, hedging effectiveness, and minimum connectedness portfolios. The findings reveal that connectedness is highly concentrated in the tails of the return distribution and intensifies during major crises, particularly the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict. The VIX, MOVE, and USD Index are generally net receivers under normal market conditions but become net transmitters during extreme market states. Clean-energy equities constitute the network core, whereas bond assets remain peripheral receivers. Portfolio results indicate that the VIX provides the most effective hedge for equity-based green assets, MOVE primarily hedges bond markets, and minimum connectedness portfolios enhance diversification by allocating capital toward less-connected assets. These findings offer practical implications for portfolio construction, dynamic hedging, and macroprudential risk management.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the collecting society regimes of Australia and New Zealand, comparing their approaches to collective copyright management. It discusses the voluntary collecting societies in New Zealand and Australia's statutory compulsory licensing schemes, particularly for educational use. The chapter analyses the similarities and differences in licensing schemes under respective Copyright Acts and explores the roles of the Copyright Tribunals in each country. It addresses the relationship between collective management and competition law, including interventions by competition authorities. The chapter provides an overview of how Copyright Tribunals determine reasonable licensing terms, their jurisdiction over licensing schemes and licensing bodies, and the balance they maintain between copyright owners' rights and users' interests.

title: Bounding a Digital Run: Realized Stablecoin Runs and CBDC Holding Limits for the Digital Euro
affiliations: Seoul National University and Seoul National University

detail.title: Bounding a Digital Run: Realized Stablecoin Runs and CBDC Holding Limits for the Digital Euro
detail.abstract: No retail CBDC run has ever occurred, so the household flight-to-safety schedule a run stress test requires has never been observed for an instrument with the CBDC's defining features, and every calibration assumes it. A retail CBDC lets depositors move into central-bank money instantly, so the digital euro proposes a per-person holding limit calibrated on that schedule. We recover the schedule from realized stablecoin runs, the closest observed flights from a digital par claim, at wallet level on the March 2023 USDC depeg, its direction confirmed on the May 2022 USDT and 2020 money-market-fund runs, replacing the assumed run process with a measured, updatable one. We then separate the stock a holding limit bounds from the flow it does not, and solve for a daily flow limit. The universal-fill assumption the ECB stresses overstates the mapped run by 1.3 to 2.3 times across mappings, and that run at a €3,000 cap is about €400bn under the holder-count mapping, conditional on the stablecoin-to-depositor transfer. The gap to an assumed legacy run-off widens as the cap rises, so a measured schedule matters most where limits rise. The run is fast, 53% on the peak day and 84% within two days, so a stock cap bounds the total but not the rate, and a €500 daily flow limit roughly halves the worst-day draw while only spreading it. If credible deposit insurance flattens sub-cap flight, the figure is high for an insured population and the overstatement larger still.

title: UNDERSTANDING FOOD INSECURITY, TERRITORIAL SPATIAL DYNAMICS, AND INEQUALITIES IN CANADA – TWO CITIES, TWO REALITIES
affiliations: Toronto Metropolitan University, University of Quebec at Rimouski, University of Quebec at Rimouski, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Toronto Metropolitan University and Toronto Metropolitan University

detail.title: UNDERSTANDING FOOD INSECURITY, TERRITORIAL SPATIAL DYNAMICS, AND INEQUALITIES IN CANADA – TWO CITIES, TWO REALITIES
detail.abstract: Food insecurity remains a persistent multidimensional challenge in Canada, where structural inequalities, racialized marginalization, and rising living costs continue to shape unequal access to adequate and culturally appropriate food. Yet, few studies have examined food insecurity from a spatial and multidimensional perspective as well as doing so through a comparative analysis. Given this, the current study fills this gap by examining the spatial patterns of food insecurity in Toronto (Ontario) and Moncton (New Brunswick) by investigating how multidimensional structural and social vulnerabilities are associated with these patterns. It achieves this objective by employing data from the Canadian Community and Health Survey and Canadian Index of Social Vulnerability (CISV). Three spatial analytical techniques are conducted—Global Moran’s I, Local Indicators of Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA), and Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR)—to identify both citywide clustering patterns and localized ones. The results highlight significant spatial structuring in both cities, with a stronger intensity observed in Moncton. It also reveals that the different dimensions of social vulnerability have different effects depending on the spatial context. This study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that food insecurity is deeply territorialized and must be understood through the articulation between social inequalities and spatial dynamics. It underscores the need for place-based public policies and interventions tailored to local contexts. Broadly, the study underscores the need for understanding food insecurity from a socio-spatial perspective in high-income countries.

title: How Does Energy Technology Innovation Improve Public Health? Evidence from the Yangtze River Delta
affiliations: Jiangsu University, Jiangsu University, Jiangsu University, Jiangsu University and Jiangsu University

detail.title: How Does Energy Technology Innovation Improve Public Health? Evidence from the Yangtze River Delta
detail.abstract: Energy technology innovation is increasingly expected to generate benefits beyond technological progress and energy conservation, yet its implications for public health and the underlying transmission mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates how energy technology innovation affects public health by integrating energy efficiency and environmental pollution into a unified analytical framework using city-level panel data from the Yangtze River Delta. Energy efficiency is evaluated using a slack-based measure (SBM), while fixed-effects models, chain-mediation analysis, bootstrap tests, robustness tests, and heterogeneity analysis are employed to examine the proposed ETI→EE→EP→PH pathway. The results suggest potential health benefits associated with energy technology innovation, although the estimated effects are not uniformly robust across alternative specifications. The contemporaneous relationship between energy technology innovation and energy efficiency is negative, and the bootstrap results do not establish a statistically significant sequential mediation effect through energy efficiency and environmental pollution. However, substantial heterogeneity is identified across cities: energy dependence constitutes the principal source of significant heterogeneity, with markedly stronger effects in high-energy-dependence cities. The co-benefit analysis further indicates that the potential energy, environmental, and health returns to technological innovation are greater in cities facing higher initial energy and environmental pressures. These findings suggest that the ETI→EE→EP→PH pathway should be interpreted as a theoretically motivated transmission framework rather than a universally confirmed mediation mechanism, and highlight the importance of differentiated policies that coordinate technological innovation, energy-efficiency improvement, pollution control, and public-health protection.

title: Mitigating the Cold-Start Problem in Digital Phenotyping: Idiographic Calibration of Deep Learning Models for Continuous Mental Health Index (MHI) Prediction
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mitigating the Cold-Start Problem in Digital Phenotyping: Idiographic Calibration of Deep Learning Models for Continuous Mental Health Index (MHI) Prediction
detail.abstract: Smartphones and wearable sensors enable continuous, passive monitoring of behavior and mental health. However, modeling behavioral data with deep learning is challenging due to high inter-individual variability, which manifests as the cold-start problem when generalizing to unseen individuals. We evaluate 8 deep learning architectures for predicting a continuousMental Health Index (MHI) derived from 7 sensor modalities in the StudentLife dataset. The architectures span four families: recurrent networks (LSTM, GRU), convolutional models (TCN), pure attention (Transformer), and hybrid architectures combining recurrent, convolutional, and attention components (CNN+GRU, CNN+LSTM, Att. BiLSTM, TFT) under temporal leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation. Under zero-shot conditions, all models exhibited negative Pooled R2 values, conrming the coldstart problem in behavioral time series. To address this, we applied an idiographic calibration strategy, ne-tuning on the rst 20% of an unseen user's data. The CNN+GRU hybrid achieved the highest post-calibration PooledR2 = 0.25 (MAE = 0.14, RMSE = 0.25), though Wilcoxon signed-rank tests showed that CNN+LSTM and Att. BiLSTM form a statistically indistinguishable top group (p > 0.05). We discuss the R2 paradox in behavioral sciences: while variance explained appears modest, the extracted temporal patterns carry practical clinical value. Our ndings support the use of hybrid architectures with active-passive sensing strategies to reduce the generalization gap in digital phenotyping.

title: Interpretable Streaming Sleep Staging via Physiologically Adaptive Test-Time Training
affiliations: Institute of Medical Informatics, University of Lübeck, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Lubeck, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Institute of Medical Informatics, University of Lübeck, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Lübeck and Institute of Medical Informatics, University of Lübeck

detail.title: Interpretable Streaming Sleep Staging via Physiologically Adaptive Test-Time Training
detail.abstract: Automated sleep stage classification using polysomnography (PSG) faces challenges in cross-site implementation due to inter-subject variability and distributional shifts. While conventional unsupervised domain adaptation methods effectively align feature spaces, they typically require offline access to large-scale unlabeled target datasets, which is often infeasible in real-time streaming scenarios. To address this, we exploit the invariance of relative, stage-discriminative frequency-band patterns to enable label-free, continuous adaptation and then propose a physiologically adaptive test-time training (PA-TTT) framework, which integrates a hierarchical 1D-convolutional neural network (CNN) encoder with a generalized additive model (GAM) output layer. It employs a knowledge-guided self-supervised task that performs stage-aware mask reconstruction on spectral band energies across physiological signals to prioritize key biomarkers. Additionally, a dual-timescale inner loop isolates slow subject-specific drift from transient fluctuations by updating only lightweight spline coefficients, while a frozen multimodal gating network dynamically balances electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), and electromyography (EMG) contributions based on source-domain reliability, preventing catastrophic drift under single-epoch updates. Upon transitioning the model from high-quality clinical data to a large-scale, heterogeneous population, PA-TTT attained an accuracy of 96.37%, a macro-averaged F1 (MF1) score of 92.14%, and a Cohen's kappa coefficient of 0.91. In reverse scenarios, the accuracy, MF1, and Cohen's kappa coefficient were 94.56%, 90.82%, and 0.89, respectively. By producing interpretable shape functions aligned with established sleep criteria, PA-TTT establishes reliable and trustworthy insights for real-world streaming sleep monitoring.

detail.abstract: Sudan's geopolitical centrality as Northeast Africa's "beating heart"controlling Nile flows, Red Sea routes, and vast resources including gold, arable land, and gum arabicrenders its stability indispensable for regional peace. Amid the 2023-2025 civil war's devastation (over 500,000 deaths, 12 million displaced, GDP contraction of 65%, inflation exceeding 1,500%), this paper analyzes the strategic imperative for the return of Islamic and national elites to governance. Critiquing post-Bashir transitional failures through elite circulation theory (Pareto, 1935), consociational democracy (Lijphart, 1977), and geopolitical realism (Morgenthau, 1948), and drawing on the core thesis of the attached Arabic document, the study proposes a 10-year mixed-economy federalism roadmap with quantitative benchmarks, risk matrices, and comparative cases (Turkey, Indonesia, Rwanda). Findings affirm that these elites possess unique capacities for national unity, security export, and multipolar balancing, thereby averting perpetual chaos in the Sahel and Horn of Africa.

title: An Equity-Effectiveness Tradeoff in Sectoral Job Training? Evidence from Year Up
affiliations: Harvard University and Boston University

detail.title: An Equity-Effectiveness Tradeoff in Sectoral Job Training? Evidence from Year Up

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The “Year Up Internal Data” used in auxiliary analysis (particularly to generate Figure A16) were provided by Year Up, which is the job-training program we analyze. Year Up is naturally an “interested” party.
declarations.funderStatement: This paper was partially funded by an HHS ACF Career Pathways Secondary Data Analysis Grant

detail.abstract: In the context of a randomized evaluation of a prominent sectoral job-training program (named Year Up), we apply machine learning techniques to study both the implications of earnings impact heterogeneity for applicant selection and potential explanations for why program impacts vary across individuals. We document that those in the top predicted impact quintile experience roughly three times the earnings boost relative to those in the bottom impact quintile. Those who benefit least are disproportionately Black, female, poor, and low-skilled, which implies an equity-effectiveness tradeoff. In particular, relative to the max impact cohort, selecting the most "disadvantaged" cohort results in an MVPF loss of approximately 16%. But, despite this, we show suggestive evidence that the program's current selection procedure results in cohorts within the equity-effectiveness frontier, potentially leaving Pareto gains on the table. We conclude by showing that the earnings impact heterogeneity is more strongly associated with predicted impacts on job quality than predicted impacts on soft skills.

title: Evaluating Urban–Rural Variation in Vehicle Fuel‑Efficiency Rebound Effects Using Household Vehicle Data
affiliations: University of Vermont and University of Vermont

detail.title: Evaluating Urban–Rural Variation in Vehicle Fuel‑Efficiency Rebound Effects Using Household Vehicle Data
detail.abstract: Vehicle fuel efficiency improvements are a key strategy for reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions but can induce a rebound effect, whereby lower driving costs increase vehicle miles traveled and offset expected GHG savings. We examine how the rebound effect varies across urban and rural contexts. Using a longitudinal dataset of 87,475 Vermont households derived from vehicle registration and inspection records, we apply household fixed‑effects models to estimate elasticities of driving with respect to fuel intensity and gasoline prices. We find that households respond more strongly to gasoline prices than to fuel efficiency, with average elasticities of −0.25 and −0.13, respectively. Both elasticities are up to four times larger in rural areas than in urban areas. These results suggest that GHG reductions from fuel efficiency improvements may be overstated in less urbanized areas and highlight the importance of accounting for geographic variation in rebound effects when evaluating transportation and climate policies.​

detail.abstract: A recent theoretical literature has given relevance to the study of the relationship between product mix changes and firm productivity. In this paper, taking advantage of a rich dataset for manufacturing plants in Chile during the period 1996-2000, we use matching techniques and a difference in difference approach to estimate the causal impact of product mix changes on productivity and other plant-specific outcomes. Our results suggest a positive and increasing impact of product mix changes on total factor productivity and labor productivity after two years the product mix changes are introduced. We also find positive effects on employment and sales. Nevertheless, this positive effect is mainly driven by firms that add and drop products at the same time. Our results are in line with recent theoretical developments on the study of productivity determinants on multiproduct firms and illustrate how products creation and destruction are a source of within-firm productivity growth.

detail.abstract: This study aims to examine whether board independence and BIG-4 auditors curb classification shifting (CS) in the business groups (BG) affiliated firms. This study uses McVay’s (2006) core earnings model as a proxy for CS. I tested the study’s hypothesis using manually collected data from 286 firms listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) for the period of 2010 to 2019.  I employed the panel data regression models with robust analysis. The results of the study show that board independence and BIG-4 auditors moderate the relationship between BG-affiliated firms and CS. The findings of the study are robust with alternative measures of CS, BG-affiliation and endogeneity problems. The results of the study provide important implications for policymakers, investors, and regulators. The evidence of this research suggests that board independence and BIG-4 auditors act as a superior deterrent in controlling CS in the BG-affiliated firms. Hence, the regulator(s) may consider the practice of CS in listed firms to protect shareholders’ interests and may focus on the line-item segregation in the income statements of their interested companies. This research study to the best of author knowledge is the first of its kind by investigating the moderating role of the BIG-4 auditors and board independence in curbing CS in the BG-affiliated firms.

detail.title: The Transaction Demand for Bitcoin

detail.abstract: A popular argument holds that because the transaction demand for Bitcoin is likely to be much higher in the future, the value of Bitcoin is likely to be much higher as well. In a Baumol-Tobin model with a binding capacity constraint on transactions, this inference fails: when Bitcoin is held on exchanges, increases in transaction demand are capitalized entirely into transaction fees, leaving the value of Bitcoin unchanged.

title: Public vs. Private Provision in Regulated Markets: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from Ambulance Services
affiliations: Bratislava University of Economics and Business and Vienna University of Technology

detail.title: Public vs. Private Provision in Regulated Markets: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from Ambulance Services
detail.abstract: We ask whether ownership affects provider performance when patients cannot choose providers and providers cannot choose patients. In Slovakia's emergency medical services, a centralized dispatch system sends the nearest available ambulance of the required type irrespective of its operator, making ownership quasi-random within narrowly defined locations. Across 2.7 million dispatches between 2020 and 2025, patients attended by public ambulances are approximately 4.5 % more likely to die before reaching a hospital than comparable patients attended by private providers - roughly 280 additional deaths per year - while non-profit providers are statistically indistinguishable from private firms. The estimate is stable across spatial resolutions from 250 metres to the municipality, robust to restricting the sample to areas where both provider types operate, to excluding calls the dispatcher had classified as arrest or apnea before assignment, and to firm-level heterogeneity within ownership groups. The gap is concentrated in urgent and critical cases, among physician-staffed crews, and outside cities. Private units also arrive faster, and the effect is largest in the years preceding the national tender through which base locations are reallocated, consistent with a response to competitive incentives and suggesting that ownership effects depend on the contractual environment in which providers operate.
